root_cause.text: Uninitialized on-stack `struct sockaddr_storage ss` in `tap_ioctl()` causes kernel stack data to be leaked to userspace because `netif_get_mac_address()` only partially fills the structure, leaving the trailing 8 bytes uninitialized.
root_cause.evidence: The commit message states that "tap_ioctl() copies 16 bytes of an uninitialised on-stack struct sockaddr_storage to userspace via ifr_hwaddr, but netif_get_mac_address() only writes sa_family and dev->addr_len (6 for Ethernet) bytes, leaving sa_data[6..13] uninitialised." The patch initializes `ss` at declaration with `= {}` to prevent the leak.

bic_trace_step.reason: In the SIOCGIFHWADDR case (line ~1000-1005), the commit declares `struct sockaddr_storage ss;` without initialization, then calls `dev_get_mac_address((struct sockaddr *)&ss, ...)`. This function may only partially fill the first 16 bytes (family + mac address), leaving the remaining 8 bytes of the passed `struct sockaddr` (and possibly more of `ss`) uninitialized. Then `copy_to_user(&ifr->ifr_hwaddr, &ss, sizeof(ifr->ifr_hwaddr))` copies 16 bytes to userspace, including the uninitialized stack data. No zeroing is performed, so the vulnerable construct is present and the fix (e.g., `struct sockaddr_storage ss = {}`) is absent.
